prompt.spicy: You're doing a task you've never done. You've been stuck for 40 minutes. The person who'd know is in a meeting for another hour.
prompt.boardroom: You are attempting an unfamiliar task and have been stuck for 40 minutes. The person who could help is in a meeting for another hour.

label.spicy: Write down exactly where you're stuck, keep trying, and send them that note if you're still stuck when they're free
label.boardroom: Document precisely where you are stuck, continue attempting it, and send that note if you are still stuck when they are free

consequence.spicy: You often solve it while writing the note down. If you don't, you've handed them a 30-second question instead of a 20-minute one.
consequence.boardroom: Articulating the blocker frequently resolves it. If not, you have converted a long conversation into a short one.

label.spicy: Move to another task and come back when they're out
label.boardroom: Move to other work and return when they are available

consequence.spicy: Nothing catches fire. But you've bought an hour of not-learning-it, and the thing is still there at 5pm.
consequence.boardroom: No damage done, though the task remains and you have gained no understanding of it.

label.spicy: Message them anyway. They can read it when they're out
label.boardroom: Message them now so they see it when the meeting ends

consequence.spicy: Fine once. Do it four times a day and you become the notification they learn to leave unread.
consequence.boardroom: Acceptable occasionally. Repeated, it trains people to deprioritise your messages.

label.spicy: Guess, do it confidently, say nothing
label.boardroom: Proceed on an assumption without flagging it

consequence.spicy: The guess is invisible until it's expensive. This is how a 40-minute problem becomes a Thursday.
consequence.boardroom: An unflagged assumption stays invisible until it is costly to unwind.

verdict.spicy: Being stuck isn't the failure. Being stuck silently and vaguely is.
verdict.boardroom: Being stuck is not a failure. Being stuck without articulating it is.

principle.spicy: Name the blocker precisely. Half of them die on contact with a sentence.
principle.boardroom: State the blocker precisely; many resolve in the act of describing them.

prompt.spicy: You've been asked to "tidy up the spreadsheet before Thursday". Nobody said why. Thursday is a client meeting.
prompt.boardroom: You have been asked to tidy a spreadsheet before Thursday. No reason was given. Thursday is a client meeting.

label.spicy: Ask what it's being used for on Thursday, then tidy it for that
label.boardroom: Ask what it will be used for on Thursday, then tidy it for that purpose

consequence.spicy: One question turns a chore into a useful thing. "Tidy" for a client means something different to "tidy" for the team.
consequence.boardroom: A single question converts an ambiguous task into a specific one. Client-ready and internally tidy are different standards.

label.spicy: Tidy it to a client-ready standard because you clocked the meeting
label.boardroom: Tidy it to a client-ready standard, inferring from the meeting

consequence.spicy: Good inference. Still a guess — and if they wanted the raw workings, you've deleted them.
consequence.boardroom: Sound inference, though still an assumption. If the workings were needed, removing them creates a problem.

label.spicy: Make it neat: colours, borders, freeze the header row
label.boardroom: Improve formatting: colour, borders, frozen header row

consequence.spicy: It looks lovely. Nobody asked for lovely. The numbers on tab 3 still contradict tab 1.
consequence.boardroom: Presentation improves while the underlying inconsistency between tabs remains.

label.spicy: Ask them to send a full spec of what "tidy" means
label.boardroom: Request a written specification of what tidy means

consequence.spicy: Now they're doing your thinking, in writing, for a spreadsheet. You've made a small task into their task.
consequence.boardroom: This transfers the thinking back to them and expands a small task into a larger one.

verdict.spicy: "Tidy" is not an instruction. Purpose is the instruction.
verdict.boardroom: Tidy is not an instruction. Purpose is the instruction.

principle.spicy: Find out what the work is for before deciding what good looks like.
principle.boardroom: Establish the purpose before defining the standard.

prompt.spicy: You notice the weekly report has had the same broken chart for three weeks. It isn't your report. Nobody's mentioned it.
prompt.boardroom: You notice the weekly report has contained the same broken chart for three weeks. It is not your report and nobody has raised it.

label.spicy: Tell the owner what's wrong, with the fix, in two lines
label.boardroom: Tell the report owner what is wrong and what the fix is, briefly

consequence.spicy: Costs you 90 seconds. Buys you a reputation as the person who notices things and isn't smug about it.
consequence.boardroom: A minimal cost that establishes you as someone who notices and communicates well.

label.spicy: Fix it yourself, quietly, in their file
label.boardroom: Correct it yourself in their file without mentioning it

consequence.spicy: The chart is fixed and the person still doesn't know they're doing it wrong. Next week: same chart.
consequence.boardroom: The immediate issue resolves, but the owner learns nothing and the error recurs.

label.spicy: Raise it in the team meeting so everyone benefits
label.boardroom: Raise it in the team meeting for the benefit of everyone

consequence.spicy: Technically efficient. Feels to them like being corrected in public over something you could've DM'd.
consequence.boardroom: Efficient in theory. In practice it reads as a public correction of something that could have been private.

label.spicy: Not your report, not your problem
label.boardroom: Take no action, as it is not your report

consequence.spicy: The report goes to the board. Someone eventually asks who spotted it. Nobody says your name.
consequence.boardroom: The error persists into senior reporting, and the opportunity is gone.

verdict.spicy: Initiative isn't doing extra work. It's routing information to whoever can act on it.
verdict.boardroom: Initiative is not additional work. It is routing information to whoever can act on it.

principle.spicy: Tell the owner. Privately. With the fix attached.
principle.boardroom: Inform the owner privately, and include the remedy.

prompt.spicy: A tool you need has thrown an error you've never seen. There's internal documentation somewhere. Probably.
prompt.boardroom: A tool you need has produced an unfamiliar error. Internal documentation exists somewhere.

label.spicy: Search the exact error text — docs, chat history, then the internet — for ten minutes
label.boardroom: Search the exact error text across documentation, chat history and the internet for ten minutes

consequence.spicy: Someone in your company has already had this error and complained about it in writing. They usually have.
consequence.boardroom: In most organisations someone has already encountered and documented this error.

label.spicy: Restart everything and try again
label.boardroom: Restart and retry

consequence.spicy: Works surprisingly often. Teaches you nothing, and the error returns on the day it matters.
consequence.boardroom: Often effective, but it produces no understanding and the error will recur.

label.spicy: Ask the team channel with a screenshot of the error
label.boardroom: Post the error in the team channel with a screenshot

consequence.spicy: Not bad — a screenshot is real information. But you skipped the ten minutes that usually ends it.
consequence.boardroom: Reasonable, and a screenshot is useful. However you have skipped the search that usually resolves it.

label.spicy: Work around it and don't mention it
label.boardroom: Work around it without reporting it

consequence.spicy: The workaround becomes permanent, undocumented, and yours forever.
consequence.boardroom: The workaround becomes permanent and undocumented, and remains your responsibility.

verdict.spicy: Ten minutes of proper searching resolves most of these. Twenty minutes of vague poking resolves none.
verdict.boardroom: Ten minutes of structured searching resolves most such errors. Unstructured effort resolves few.

principle.spicy: Search the exact string. Not your description of the string.
principle.boardroom: Search the exact error text, not a paraphrase of it.

prompt.spicy: You can't deliver both the analysis and the deck by Friday. You need to say so.
prompt.boardroom: You cannot deliver both the analysis and the deck by Friday and need to raise it.

label.spicy: "I can have the analysis done Thursday, but not the deck as well. Can the deck move to Tuesday, or should I get someone on it?"
label.boardroom: "I can complete the analysis by Thursday but not the deck as well. Can the deck move to Tuesday, or should it be reassigned?"

consequence.spicy: Two options, a real constraint, and something for them to say yes to. This gets granted almost every time.
consequence.boardroom: A stated constraint with two viable options. Requests in this form are usually granted.

label.spicy: "Friday's tight for both. Which one do you actually need first?"
label.boardroom: "Friday is tight for both. Which do you need first?"

consequence.spicy: Honest and answerable. You've made them do the sequencing you could've proposed.
consequence.boardroom: Clear and answerable, though it asks them to do prioritisation you could have proposed.

label.spicy: "This workload isn't really sustainable."
label.boardroom: "The current workload is not sustainable."

consequence.spicy: True, possibly urgent, and completely un-actionable. It gets filed as a mood, not a request.
consequence.boardroom: Possibly accurate but not actionable. It registers as sentiment rather than a request.

label.spicy: Say nothing, do both badly, mention it Friday at 4:58pm
label.boardroom: Say nothing, attempt both, and raise it late on Friday

consequence.spicy: Two weak deliverables and a surprise. The surprise is the part they'll remember.
consequence.boardroom: Two substandard deliverables plus a late surprise, which is the part that is remembered.

verdict.spicy: "I'm struggling" is a feeling. "Move the deck to Tuesday" is a request. Only one of them can be granted.
verdict.boardroom: A statement of difficulty is not a request. Only a specific proposal can be granted.

principle.spicy: Name the constraint, propose the trade, leave them something to say yes to.
principle.boardroom: Name the constraint, propose the trade-off, and leave a decision that can be approved.

prompt.spicy: Your mistake made it into something a client saw. You found it. Nobody else has.
prompt.boardroom: An error you made reached a client-facing document. You identified it; nobody else has.

label.spicy: Flag it now: what happened, what's affected, what you've already done about it
label.boardroom: Raise it immediately: what occurred, what is affected, and the action already taken

consequence.spicy: Uncomfortable for four minutes. It's also the single fastest way to be trusted with bigger things.
consequence.boardroom: Briefly uncomfortable, and the most reliable route to being trusted with more.

label.spicy: Fix it, then flag it once the fix is in
label.boardroom: Correct it, then raise it once the correction is in place

consequence.spicy: Defensible. The risk is the delay: if someone else finds it first, the story is now about the gap.
consequence.boardroom: Defensible, but the delay carries risk. If discovered independently, the delay becomes the issue.

label.spicy: Explain the process problem that made it likely
label.boardroom: Explain the process weakness that contributed to it

consequence.spicy: The process point might be correct. Leading with it sounds like a defence lawyer opening a case.
consequence.boardroom: The observation may be valid, but leading with it reads as deflection.

label.spicy: Say nothing. It might never come up
label.boardroom: Take no action in the hope it is not identified

consequence.spicy: If it surfaces later — and it does — the mistake stops being the problem. You concealing it becomes the problem.
consequence.boardroom: If it emerges later, the concealment rather than the error becomes the issue.

verdict.spicy: Own the fact, not the identity. "I got the figure wrong, here's the fix" — not "I'm so useless".
verdict.boardroom: Take responsibility for the fact, not through self-criticism. State the error and the remedy.

principle.spicy: Accountability is naming your part without collapsing into it.
principle.boardroom: Accountability is naming your part without collapsing.

prompt.spicy: Third week of genuinely dull work. Sleep is fine, health is fine, you're just bored and slightly resentful.
prompt.boardroom: You are three weeks into genuinely dull work. Your health and sleep are fine; you are bored and somewhat resentful.

label.spicy: Do it, and get better at doing it fast — then use the time you save
label.boardroom: Complete it while improving your speed at it, and use the time recovered

consequence.spicy: Boring work is where the automation ideas live. Also where people notice who doesn't need chasing.
consequence.boardroom: Routine work reveals improvement opportunities, and reliability on it is highly visible.

label.spicy: Do it, and ask what you could take on next
label.boardroom: Complete it and ask what you could take on next

consequence.spicy: Reasonable. Slightly risky if the current work isn't finished — you look like you're shopping.
consequence.boardroom: Reasonable, though premature if current work is incomplete.

label.spicy: Tell your manager you're not being challenged
label.boardroom: Tell your manager you are not being sufficiently challenged

consequence.spicy: Three weeks in, this reads as "I'd like the interesting bits without doing the boring bits". Sometimes fair. Rarely lands.
consequence.boardroom: At three weeks this reads as wanting the interesting work without the routine work.

label.spicy: Slow down. Match the energy of the task
label.boardroom: Reduce your pace in line with the interest level of the task

consequence.spicy: Boredom becomes visible as unreliability. Nobody can see the difference from outside.
consequence.boardroom: From the outside, disengagement is indistinguishable from unreliability.

verdict.spicy: Bored isn't distressed. Bored is most jobs, some of the time, and it's where capacity gets built.
verdict.boardroom: Boredom is not distress. It is a normal component of most work and a place capacity is built.

principle.spicy: Calibrate: is this hard, unpleasant, or actually harmful? Three different responses.
principle.boardroom: Calibrate whether something is difficult, unpleasant, or harmful. Each warrants a different response.

prompt.spicy: You've been sleeping badly for a month, can't concentrate, and stopped doing the things you used to like. Deadline on Friday.
prompt.boardroom: For the past month you have slept poorly, struggled to concentrate, and lost interest in things you previously enjoyed. There is a deadline on Friday.

label.spicy: Book a doctor, and tell your manager what needs to move this week — not why
label.boardroom: Arrange medical advice, and tell your manager what needs to move this week without disclosing the reason

consequence.spicy: A month of dropped functioning isn't a mindset problem and grit doesn't fix it. You also don't owe anyone the details.
consequence.boardroom: A sustained drop in functioning is a clinical matter, not a motivational one. Detail is not owed to an employer.

label.spicy: Tell your manager you need the deadline moved and sort the rest after
label.boardroom: Ask for the deadline to move and address the rest afterwards

consequence.spicy: The immediate pressure comes off, which matters. The month-long part is still a month long.
consequence.boardroom: Immediate pressure reduces, but the underlying issue remains unaddressed.

label.spicy: Push through until Friday and reassess after
label.boardroom: Continue until Friday and reassess afterwards

consequence.spicy: There is always another Friday. That's the mechanism by which this goes on for a year.
consequence.boardroom: There is always a subsequent deadline, which is how such periods extend indefinitely.

label.spicy: Read about productivity systems and try a new one
label.boardroom: Adopt a new productivity system

consequence.spicy: You cannot out-system a month of not sleeping.
consequence.boardroom: No system compensates for a month of impaired sleep and concentration.

verdict.spicy: Discomfort is trainable. Functioning that dropped and stayed dropped is medical. Scoring high here means telling them apart — not pushing through.
verdict.boardroom: Discomfort is trainable. A sustained drop in functioning is medical. Correctly distinguishing the two is the skill being measured.

principle.spicy: Escalating genuine overload correctly is a high score, not a low one.
principle.boardroom: Correctly escalating genuine overload is a strong response, not a weak one.

prompt.spicy: In a meeting, you're mid-sentence and your manager says "let's park that" in a slightly flat voice. Two clients are on the call.
prompt.boardroom: During a client call, your manager interrupts your point with "let's park that", in a notably flat tone.

label.spicy: Stop immediately, move on, and raise it with them afterwards
label.boardroom: Stop, move on, and follow up with them privately afterwards

consequence.spicy: "Park that" with clients present almost always means "not in front of them". You'll get the reason in private.
consequence.boardroom: In client settings this usually signals a timing issue rather than a disagreement. The rationale follows privately.

label.spicy: Finish the sentence briefly, then move on
label.boardroom: Complete the point concisely, then move on

consequence.spicy: You get the point out. You also just told the clients there's a disagreement in the room.
consequence.boardroom: The point is made, but it signals internal disagreement to the client.

label.spicy: Ask why it's being parked
label.boardroom: Ask why the point is being deferred

consequence.spicy: A completely fair question. Asked here, in front of clients, it becomes a scene.
consequence.boardroom: A legitimate question, but asked in front of clients it becomes a visible disagreement.

label.spicy: Go quiet for the rest of the call and think about it for four days
label.boardroom: Withdraw for the remainder of the call and reflect on it at length

consequence.spicy: The clients notice. Your manager notices. Nobody knows what happened, including you, because you never asked.
consequence.boardroom: The withdrawal is visible to everyone and the reason is never established, because it is never asked.

verdict.spicy: Same words, different room, different meaning. Audience is part of the message.
verdict.boardroom: The same words carry different meaning depending on who is present. Audience is part of the message.

principle.spicy: Read who's in the room before you decide what was said.
principle.boardroom: Account for who is present before interpreting what was said.

prompt.spicy: You did the work and sent it three days ago. No reply. It's needed for something on Monday.
prompt.boardroom: You completed and sent the work three days ago with no response. It is required for Monday.

label.spicy: Follow up with a deadline in it: "Assuming no changes, I'll send this on to Priya Friday 3pm"
label.boardroom: Follow up with a stated default: "Unless I hear otherwise I will pass this to Priya at 3pm Friday"

consequence.spicy: Silence now means yes. You've closed the loop without needing them to do anything.
consequence.boardroom: Silence becomes consent and the loop closes without requiring action from them.

label.spicy: Send a polite nudge
label.boardroom: Send a polite reminder

consequence.spicy: Might work. "Just bumping this" is a request for attention with no decision attached to it.
consequence.boardroom: It may work, but a reminder without a proposed default requires them to initiate.

label.spicy: It's sent. Your part is done
label.boardroom: Consider your part complete, as it has been sent

consequence.spicy: Sending is activity. Monday is the outcome. Only one of those is your job.
consequence.boardroom: Sending is activity; Monday is the outcome. The outcome is the responsibility.

label.spicy: Escalate to their manager
label.boardroom: Escalate to their manager

consequence.spicy: Effective exactly once, at a price. Three days and one follow-up doesn't earn it.
consequence.boardroom: Effective but costly, and not warranted after three days and no follow-up.

verdict.spicy: Closing the loop is the job. Sending the email is the beginning of the job.
verdict.boardroom: Closing the loop is the work. Sending the email begins it.

principle.spicy: Put a default in the follow-up so silence becomes an answer.
principle.boardroom: Include a default in the follow-up so that silence resolves it.

prompt.spicy: You're certain the plan is wrong. You've said so once. It's been decided. You're still certain.
prompt.boardroom: You believe the plan is wrong. You have said so once. The decision has been made and your view has not changed.

label.spicy: Commit to it properly, and write down the specific thing you expect to go wrong and when
label.boardroom: Commit fully, and record the specific failure you expect and its likely timing

consequence.spicy: You execute in good faith and you have a dated, specific note. That note is how you get listened to next time.
consequence.boardroom: You execute in good faith while creating a specific, dated record. That record is what earns influence later.

label.spicy: Ask for one more conversation with your reasoning written down
label.boardroom: Request one further discussion, with your reasoning documented

consequence.spicy: Legitimate once. Twice and it stops being judgement and starts being a campaign.
consequence.boardroom: Legitimate on one occasion. Repeated, it reads as relitigating rather than judgement.

label.spicy: Do it, but slightly your way where nobody's checking
label.boardroom: Implement it with unapproved modifications where they are unlikely to be noticed

consequence.spicy: Now the plan can't be evaluated, because it was never actually run. You've destroyed the evidence you needed.
consequence.boardroom: The plan can no longer be assessed, because it was not implemented as agreed.

label.spicy: Do it, and make sure people know you disagreed
label.boardroom: Implement it while ensuring others know you objected

consequence.spicy: This is pre-building an alibi. Everyone can see it, and it costs you more than the failure would have.
consequence.boardroom: This is visible pre-emptive distancing, and it costs more credibility than the outcome would.

verdict.spicy: Being right isn't the same as being useful. Disagree, commit, and be specific about what you predicted.
verdict.boardroom: Being correct is not the same as being useful. Disagree, commit, and record a specific prediction.

principle.spicy: A dated, specific prediction is worth ten retrospective "I said so"s.
principle.boardroom: A specific, dated prediction carries far more weight than retrospective objection.

prompt.spicy: Six months in. Nobody has told you what "good" looks like in this role, and nobody is going to.
prompt.boardroom: Six months into the role, no one has defined what good performance looks like, and no one is likely to.

label.spicy: Write your own version, take it to your manager, ask what's missing
label.boardroom: Draft your own definition, take it to your manager, and ask what is missing

consequence.spicy: Editing someone's draft is easy. Producing one from nothing is not. You've made it easy for them to say yes.
consequence.boardroom: Reviewing a draft is straightforward; producing one is not. This makes agreement easy.

label.spicy: Ask your manager directly what good looks like
label.boardroom: Ask your manager directly what good performance looks like

consequence.spicy: Fine, and often gets a vague answer, because they haven't written it down either.
consequence.boardroom: Reasonable, though it frequently yields a general answer, as it is often undefined for them too.

label.spicy: Copy whoever seems most respected around here
label.boardroom: Model your approach on the most respected person in the team

consequence.spicy: Decent instinct, imperfect data. You're copying what's visible, which is rarely the part that matters.
consequence.boardroom: A reasonable instinct based on incomplete information; visible behaviour is rarely the decisive part.

label.spicy: Wait for the performance review to find out
label.boardroom: Wait for the formal review to establish it

consequence.spicy: You'll find out what good looked like at the exact moment it's too late to have done it.
consequence.boardroom: The standard becomes clear only when it is too late to have met it.

verdict.spicy: Your role is being defined whether you're in the room or not. Bring a draft.
verdict.boardroom: The role is being defined regardless of your involvement. Bring a draft.

principle.spicy: Write the version you want reviewed. Blank pages get filled in by other people.
principle.boardroom: Produce the version you want reviewed; otherwise others will define it.
